newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU wheat tax cut may not make exports competitive.
newsitem.headline: EU wheat tax cut may not make exports competitive.

text.p: Tim Hepher
News the EU is considering a further cut in European Union wheat and flour export taxes sent officials and traders back to the rule books to gauge the effect on prices.
The short answer is that abolishing the wheat export tax would do little to make EU wheat competitive, leaving late August new-crop French wheat about $12 above U.S. soft red winter, traders said.
It would however compete against higher priced U.S. hard red winter, in price if not in quality.
But there was less agreement about whether it would be a move towards lifting an effective export ban or simply bowing to the inevitable at a politically convenient moment.
EU Commission sources in Brussels said earlier the EU's grain panel, which meets this afternoon, might cut or scrap the controversial five Ecu per tonne tax. There was no immediate confirmation.
"People would definitely see this as a signal they are getting ready to export," said one member country official.
The Commission has delayed the start of exports from this year's harvest due to fears of drought damage, though prospects have improved.

But others said it would make little difference to the international market, which was waiting for the EU to open weekly export tenders for the 1997/98 campaign. These would almost certainly push the EU directly back to export subsidies.

Any cut in the tax would apply to the EU's alternative daily export channel which can be more difficult to anticipate. If pushed through today, it would ease friction with the United States in time for high-level farm talks in Washington on Monday and dampen a row with France, whose new Socialist leadership opposed the tax.
Even if the tax stays, the prospect of a change has at least allowed traders and officials to clear up confusion over the way any future abolition would be applied.
If the EU were to turn the five Ecus tax into a zero Ecu refund, several arcane sections of the EU rule book would come into play and start cancelling each other out.

Traders would get a licence valid for the usual current month plus four months -- until end-October -- and the value of the licence would be raised by bonuses of 1.1 Ecus per month from August until it was used.
Yet if a licence was issued in one campaign and used in another, a "change of campaign" penalty of around 11 Ecus would have to be taken off again.
But EU rules allow the value of the licence to be held at zero in such a case, rather than going into negative territory, which would be tantamount to a higher tax than the original one.
So any trader who applied for such a licence should end up with a paper valid for almost five months at a guaranteed zero.
The rules would have taken the licence from zero to one or two Ecus, then deep into tax territory and finally back to zero.

Officials said one last wrinkle might be that so-called correctives -- variations in refunds for individual months -- currently have no value. In EU jargon "no value" means a penalty can be imposed later.
But several traders and officials said they believed even a change in the "corrective" could not cut a licence below zero.
One official said if the Commission wanted to abolish the tax, it would probably prefer to do so in two stages.

It would put wheat export refunds at "no value" first -- like a zero refund but not fixed and only valid for 30 days -- and then go back to a zero refund with full validity the following week. This would be a first step to reopening exports but need not signal immediate sales.
